subject: jukebox
pitch: A 1950s diner jukebox. A tall rounded arch of glowing coloured tubes in red, amber and teal, chrome trim everywhere, a domed glass window showing a stack of records and the arm that picks them, rows of chrome selection buttons with little title cards, a speaker grille with a starburst pattern, and a coin slot.
reasoning:
I'm designing a 1950s Wurlitzer-style jukebox prop, roughly 1.5m tall by 1m wide by 0.65m deep, starting with a root joint at the origin and planning out the base plinth and overall layout facing forward.

Working through the structure from bottom to top: a dark chrome kick-plate plinth, then a lower speaker-grille section with a starburst paint pattern generated procedurally using radial rays, concentric rings, and perforation dots computed from surface position and normal.

For texture quality, I'm bumping the paint sheet resolution to 2048 for a crisper starburst, estimating texel density based on total painted area to keep detail sharp. I'm also considering using SVG textures for decorative title cards, noting these render properly in-browser but stay blank under Node, so I should treat them as a browser-side enhancement rather than a core requirement.

I'm planning the control panel layout with a budget of roughly 1000 parts and 60k triangles, using rows of small chrome cylinder buttons with colored caps. For the main silhouette, I'm designing the iconic Wurlitzer-style arch as concentric colored tube sweeps—red outer, amber middle, teal inner—framed by chrome trim bands, aiming for a glowing effect around the dome window using emissive materials.

Since the material system shares cached materials by color string, I realize I can grab the shared material for each tube color and bump its emissive and emissiveIntensity directly to get the glow without needing a separate emissive color parameter. For the chrome trim, I'm weighing metalness and roughness values carefully since without an environment map, high metalness tends to render too dark—so I'm leaning toward a moderate metalness with a light base color to avoid a flat black chrome look.

For the glass dome, I'm planning to mark its material transparent with low opacity and disable depth-write to avoid z-fighting, using a dedicated color key so I can tune it without affecting other parts. Now I'm moving into actual dimensions for the jukebox cabinet, setting overall height, width, and depth in meters before laying out the profile shape.

I'm figuring out the tombstone silhouette: a rectangular lower body transitioning into a rounded arch at the top, computing the arch radius and center so the straight sides blend smoothly into the semicircle. I'm planning to build this body as an extruded outline along the front-facing plane, defining the orientation axes so the extrusion comes out facing forward, then working out the explicit arc points for the outline starting from the bottom corners.

Now I'm thinking through the color palette for the cabinet -- considering a 1950s jukebox aesthetic with cream, chrome, and deep lacquer tones, weighing whether a darker burgundy or cream body would make the glowing red, amber, and teal tubes in the arch pop more against it.

I'm sketching out the physical structure piece by piece: a plinth at the base with a chrome kick strip, then the main cream-colored tombstone body extruded upward with beveled edges, and planning a dark navy inset panel on the front where the dome window and glowing tube arch will sit, plus chrome trim along the side edges to tie it together.

I'm weighing whether to paint the body with a hard-edged two-tone stripe (teal lower, cream upper, hidden seam under a chrome band) versus building it from separate colored pieces, and running through the atlas texel density math to make sure the painted body and starburst grille details stay sharp enough without wasting texture space.

I'm now leaning toward splitting the body into simpler, crisper parts instead: a lower cabinet box and a separate upper arched body section. I'm sketching out a color palette — cream, glowing red/amber/teal, chrome, dark, burgundy — and deciding to go with a cream body, chrome trim on the sides, a burgundy button deck, and a starburst grille panel in dark/gold over a teal base, then starting to lay out the front panel heights section by section.

Now I'm working through the speaker grille dimensions and chrome frame, then figuring out the selector deck above it — a tilted panel with two rows of chrome buttons and title cards, plus placement of the coin slot and return cup. I'm working out which side of the deck should hold the coin mechanism, reasoning through the model's orientation versus the viewer's perspective to get the left/right placement correct.

Working out the deck's tilt normal and plane basis vectors so I can place buttons correctly, then figuring out how BoxGeometry's UV mapping on the top face aligns with the card texture for the title cards.

Rather than reason through text orientation manually, I realize I can just use a standard PlaneGeometry (which faces +Z with image-up along +Y) and rotate it with a quaternion to match the deck's tilt normal, solving for the rotation angle about X that maps +Z to the deck normal while keeping +Y as "up" for the viewer. That gives a clean rotation formula I can apply to each deck part.

I'm also thinking about building deck elements using local coordinates where +Z always points outward, then placing them via rotation -- so buttons and other cylinders get rotated 90° about X to point along +Z instead of the default +Y axis. I'm considering using a Region abstraction with its own quaternion so deck parts can be placed in local deck-space coordinates, letting the region handle composing rotations automatically.

I'll stick with the deck region and reuse shared geometry objects across repeated parts like the title cards, since three.js handles shared geometry fine as long as nothing mutates it directly.

Now I'm turning to the glowing arch of tubes framing the dome window at the front of the cabinet—working out the radii and spacing for the colored tube rings (red, amber, etc.) that need to frame the dome window based on the actual Wurlitzer 1015 design.

I'm picturing the Wurlitzer 1015's rainbow bubble tubes: nested arch tubes in red, amber, and teal running up, over, and down the sides, plus possibly a pair of vertical side tubes as pilasters. I'm constructing the U-shaped arch path as a sequence of points—straight sides rising up, then curving over the top—to sweep a tube mesh along.

Alternatively, I'm considering building the arch manually as a rotational path, working out the correct rotation axis and direction so the arc sweeps from the left anchor point clockwise over the top to the right anchor point, verifying the rotation math with Rodrigues' formula to make sure the orientation is correct.
